analysis.one_liner: Lets employers pay individual workers more than their union contract allows.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law so that a union's contract could not stop an employer from paying any individual worker more than the negotiated wage scale. Supporters framed it as letting employers reward high performers. Unions view this type of change as a way for management to sidestep the single wage scale a union negotiates for everyone, by paying selected workers more while leaving the contract otherwise untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with unionized workforces gain a new tool: the freedom to pay any employee above the union-contracted scale without renegotiating it. Individual unionized workers whom management chooses to reward would receive higher pay than their contract provides. Other employees in the unit would not see any change to the contract itself.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act so that nothing in the law's ban on employer interference with collective bargaining — nor the terms of any union contract — could stop an employer from paying an individual worker higher wages than the contract provides.

In practice, this would let a company reward specific employees — high performers, scarce skills, or simply favored workers — with above-scale pay, rather than paying everyone on the single scale negotiated in the union contract.

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose part of their control over the wage structure, since an employer could pay selected workers outside the scale the union negotiated. Unionized workforces collectively would bear the risk of a divided pay structure: if management can reward some workers above scale, the shared standard that binds members together in bargaining is easier to erode, and workers the employer does not favor could lose leverage.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives management a way to pay around the union contract without bargaining over it. Opponents of this type of amendment argue it lets an employer divide a unionized workforce — rewarding favored employees while the negotiated scale for everyone else stays frozen — which weakens the union's ability to bargain as a single unit.

Any individual raise depends entirely on the employer's discretion. A worker only benefits if management chooses to pay above scale, so the bill creates no right or guarantee of higher pay for anyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrow: some individual workers could earn more than their contract scale, if their employer decides so. The structural change is larger than the individual raises it might produce, because it hands employers a tool to pay around a negotiated agreement. For a unionized workforce, the value of collective bargaining rests on one shared scale; letting management pay select individuals above it, outside of bargaining, is a genuine erosion of that. Whether the individual raises outweigh the loss of bargaining leverage depends on how a given employer uses the power — the bill offers no safeguard either way.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Todd Rokita introduced the bill on February 9, 2017, joined by five other Republicans as original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing rules stayed in place: unions kept full control over the wage scales they negotiate, and employers gained no new power to pay around a contract. No worker's pay changed as a result.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions and the bargaining status quo

for.name: Rep. Todd Rokita
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let employers pay workers above their union-contracted wage scale.

for.name: 6 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce (Chair Virginia Foxx)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for consideration, so it died in committee.

against.name: Labor unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed this type of amendment as a way for management to undermine negotiated wage scales; their opposition did not need to be exercised because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would give management a way to pay individual employees above the union scale without renegotiating the contract — a flexibility employers' groups have long sought. It creates no obligation to raise anyone's pay, and its most likely use is selective above-scale pay that weakens the bargained standard.

A union's core product is a single wage scale negotiated for all members; letting employers pay around that scale for chosen workers erodes the union's control over pay structure and its cohesion in bargaining. Unions' interest here runs alongside their members' collective stake in an enforced contract.
